originalTitle: Britain’s Amy Hunt powers to emphatic 100m European gold to thrill home crowd
summary: The British sprinter secured the 100m European title in 11.00sec in Birmingham, with Ewa Swoboda claiming silver and Delphine Nkansa a bronze
content: After a display of icy resolve and sustained power had secured Amy Hunt a European 100m gold medal, Britain’s new sprint queen reached for a Freddie Mercury lyric. “I want it all,” she said, before peering into a golden future. The Cambridge graduate, 24, now plans to leave the European Championships with four gold medals, adding the 200m and 4x100m women’s and mixed relays to her 100m title. On this evidence, would you dare bet against her? Hunt is never the quickest starter. In truth, she reacted to the gun like a woman whose spikes had been superglued to her blocks and she was still behind with 30m to go before coming through to take her first major title in 11.00sec. “I’ve probably had much worse starts than that,” Hunt said. “The biggest thing is not panicking, trusting in my very, very long legs, long femurs, and just staying calm and pulling through at the end. “‘Trash’ is probably going to be his [her coach, Marco Airale] words about my start,” she said. “And maybe a little bit of Italian blasphemy, but we came through at the end. One of my biggest skills in terms of championships is I know I’m so strong in the end and I always have that kind of extra magic in the last 40, 50m.” Ewa Swoboda of Poland secured silver in 11.02, while Delphine Nkansa took bronze for Belgium in 11.06. “Honestly, it’s just euphoria,” said Hunt. “My first gold. I think it was definitely time to upgrade. This was definitely a coming of age for me. I’m someone that thrives under that pressure, so the stage for the final isn’t intimidating to me. I just knew I had to stay calm and not overthink myself into the gold before I had it in my grasp.” It was also sweet vindication after being beaten into silver at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow a fortnight ago. “It really came in handy for me,” she said. “I wanted to have that experience of being in front of a home crowd and having that meta-expectation, because I’ve never had that before. I took a lot of learnings from Glasgow into today and it really helped me. Hunt’s story loses little in its retelling. She was the world’s fastest woman over 200m at 18, then had a series of injuries that got so bad some questioned whether she would ever fulfil her potential. A few years ago she ruptured one of her quadriceps so badly that her mum needed to lift her out of the shower. When she won a 200m silver medal in Tokyo last year, she called herself a “track goddess and an academic badass”. “I don’t know if I have any more one-liners in me,” she said. Then came the Freddie Mercury line. Hunt later revealed she had a premonition that she was going to win gold. “I just had such a magical feeling,” she said. “I’ve won English Schools here. I’ve raced here as 13-14-year-old. So, this is really my track. I’m a girl from Newark, I’m a Midlands girl. So I just had a feeling that this was going to be my night.” Hunt insisted that this could be just the start as she now chases an historic four gold medals. “I want to be the best,” she said. “I don’t shy away from that. I train incredibly hard, and I back myself so incredibly hard because I do want to be the best. “I’m not saying that I’m the best right now, but that’s something I aspire to be.” Hunt said she was so nervous before the race that she was unable to nap. Instead, she was just lay awake in bed with her eyes closed. “But I as soon as I get to the track, my nerves disappear,” she said. “I love doing what I do. My coach keeps me really chilled. Megan Thee Stallion [American rapper] kept me kind of nice and upbeat, and you can’t be nervous when you listen to that.” She also relaxed by playing puzzle games such as Connections, Spelling Bee, Pips and Wordle. “It wakes my brain up without having to overthink. “Even at training, we’re all competitive every single day about Wordle and how many kind of words we got on Spelling Bee, so it just keeps my brain ticking over, listening to Megan Thee Stallion, house music, a bit of Mamma Mia in there, so just not getting too overly serious.” Moments before Hunt’s victory there was also a plucky silver for Great Britain’s mixed 4x400m relay team behind the gold medallists Norway. Britain’s team of Ben Jefferies, Charlotte Henrich, Toby Harries and Yemi Mary John all ran well. But a Norway team spearheaded by the 400m hurdles world record-holder, Karsten Warholm, and the fastest woman in Europe this year, Henriette Jæger, proved too strong as they set a Championship record of 3:09.62, nearly a second clear of Britain. The only disappointment was that more people were not here to witness it given that the Alexander Stadium, which seats about 20,000, looked barely half full. However, organisers said 13,623 tickets had been sold for the Monday night – along with 170,000 tickets for the week – and that from Thursday night onwards the event was pretty much a sellout.
chineseTitle: 英国选手艾米·亨特 (Amy Hunt) 斩获 1 亿欧洲金牌，让家乡观众兴奋不已
chineseSummary: 这位英国短跑运动员在伯明翰以 11 秒的成绩获得了 100 米欧洲冠军，埃瓦·斯沃博达 (Ewa Swoboda) 获得银牌，德尔芬·恩坎萨 (Delphine Nkansa) 获得铜牌
chineseContent: 在艾米·亨特 (Amy Hunt) 凭借冰冷的决心和持久的力量赢得了欧洲 100 米金牌后，这位英国新的短跑女王又唱起了弗雷迪·墨丘里 (Freddie Mercury) 的歌词。 “我想要这一切，”她在展望金色未来之前说道。这位 24 岁的剑桥毕业生现在计划带着四枚金牌离开欧洲锦标赛，在她的 100 米冠军头衔中增加 200 米和 4x100 米女子接力以及混合接力。就凭这个证据，你还敢跟她打赌吗？亨特从来都不是最快的首发者。事实上，她对枪的反应就像一个钉鞋被强力粘在她的积木上的女人一样，在还剩 30m 的时候她仍然落后，然后在 11 秒内夺得了她的第一个大满贯冠军。 “我的开局可能比这糟糕得多，”亨特说。 “最重要的是不要惊慌，相信我非常非常长的腿和长股骨，保持冷静并在最后坚持下去。“‘垃圾’可能会是他（她的教练马可·艾拉勒）对我的开始的评价，”她说。“也许有一点意大利式的亵渎，但我们最终还是挺了过来。在冠军方面，我最大的技能之一是我知道自己最终非常强大，而且在最后 40、50m 中我总是拥有那种额外的魔力。”波兰选手埃瓦·斯沃博达 (Ewa Swoboda) 以 11.02 秒获得银牌，比利时选手德尔芬·恩坎萨 (Delphine Nkansa) 以 11.06 秒获得铜牌。 “老实说，这只是一种欣快感，”亨特说。 “我的第一枚金牌。我认为现在绝对是升级的时候了。这对我来说绝对是一个成熟的时刻。我是一个在这种压力下茁壮成长的人，所以决赛的舞台对我来说并不可怕。我只知道在获得金牌之前我必须保持冷静，不要过度思考自己是否能获得金牌。”这也是两周前在格拉斯哥英联邦运动会上获得银牌后的甜蜜辩护。 “这对我来说真的很有用
